product: Payday loan, title loan, personal loan, or advance loan
issue: Problem with additional add-on products or services

themes.label: Financed goods or services not delivered as represented
themes.description: Consumers allege a merchant or contractor misrepresented, failed to complete, or stopped providing financed goods, services, or programs, while the lender kept billing.

examples.summary: Consumer claims they obtained a loan for solar installation, but the contractor failed to complete the work beyond the contract deadline and ceased operations, leaving the consumer to finish the project at their own expense and effort.

Consumer claims a lease for a product with a materially misrepresented description was enforced despite the consumer's written rejection of the goods and attempt to cancel, with the creditor threatening to proceed with billing unless the merchant releases the obligation.

Consumer claims they purchased an add-on warranty with their loan but were unable to obtain warranty support, repairs, or inspection due to conflicting directions between the warranty provider and finance company.

themes.label: Lender or BNPL dispute handling failures
themes.description: Consumers allege the lender or pay-later provider did not properly investigate, reopen, or resolve disputes over merchandise, services, or balances.

examples.summary: Consumer disputes remaining balance on financed services allegedly not fully completed and claims creditor failed to conduct reasonable investigation into the dispute despite contradictory findings.
Consumer claims that a third party refused to credit $76.00 for returned merchandise despite receiving and acknowledging delivery of the items, citing that a claim was opened with Affirm.

A consumer claims Klarna refused to reopen or investigate a dispute for allegedly defective merchandise, stating the system was locked after the consumer closed an initial delivery dispute, and directed the consumer to resolve the matter with an unresponsive merchant.

themes.label: Undisclosed terms and questionable loan origination
themes.description: Consumers allege add-ons, fees, signatures, advertised credits, or marketing were not clearly disclosed, authorized, or honored when the loan was offered or originated.

examples.summary: Consumer claims that optional add-on products totaling over $3000 were added to an auto loan without clear disclosure as optional, that electronic signatures were executed on documents the consumer was never shown and did not authorize, and that the vehicle's history and prior accident damage were misrepresented at sale.

Consumer received an unsolicited mailer from a lender containing a document designed to resemble a check and a personalized URL, and claims the mailer uses deceptive practices by mimicking check-style design and allegedly misdirecting consumers from advertised loans to debt-relief products.
Consumer claims they were charged for undisclosed or unauthorized add-on products on a personal loan and subsequently faced default judgment and collection action after job loss.

themes.label: Account access, servicing and collection conduct
themes.description: Consumers allege problems with closing accounts, accessing funds, privacy, loan transfers, or contact and collection practices after the loan was made.

examples.summary: Consumer claims a payday lender sold the loan to a third-party collection agency and added CFPB-ordered penalty fees to the balance owed rather than complying with the ruling.

Consumer claims a peer-to-peer loan marketplace refused to close their account or delete personal data after multiple requests, requiring SMS verification to a phone number they no longer have access to and declining to offer alternative verification methods.

Consumer claims a lender withheld access to cash advances and failed to return residual funds or provide account documentation despite multiple requests, while providing inconsistent explanations for the account restrictions.

brief.headline: Financed purchase disputes rising, with BNPL and point-of-sale lenders over-represented
brief.what_is_happening: Complaints in this cluster are running above the prior baseline, at 149.67 per month in the last three months versus 130.17 in the baseline period (velocity 1.1443, rank 10 of 79). Monthly counts stepped up from 101 in 2025-12 to 137 in 2026-01 and have stayed between 122 and 156 since. Consumers claim that financed goods, services or add-ons were not delivered as represented, that disputes were not investigated or reopened, and that fees or add-ons were not clearly disclosed. These are unverified allegations.
brief.who_is_affected: Consumers who financed purchases through buy-now-pay-later, point-of-sale, solar, auto and personal loan products, and who dispute the underlying merchant's performance. Complaints are concentrated in TX (15.0%), FL (12.3%) and CA (11.6%). In the AI-reviewed sample, 6.1% of consumers showed signs of vulnerability.
brief.likely_root_cause: Hypothesis to test: lenders and BNPL providers may lack a clear way to treat a failed or misrepresented merchant transaction as a billing dispute, so they may keep billing or direct consumers back to merchants who are unresponsive or defunct. A second hypothesis is that add-on products and fees are not clearly disclosed or consented to at origination. Both would need validation against internal dispute and origination records.
brief.process_or_control_to_check: Check the dispute intake and investigation workflow for financed merchant disputes, including rules for reopening closed disputes and handling defunct merchants. Also check origination disclosure and e-signature consent controls for add-on products, third-party merchant and contractor oversight, and account closure and identity verification procedures.
brief.regulatory_area: Consumer credit dispute handling and add-on product disclosure in point-of-sale, buy-now-pay-later and personal lending
evidence: Recent monthly average of 149.67 complaints versus 130.17 in the baseline, a velocity of 1.1443 ranking 10 of 79.
Monthly complaints rose from 101 in 2025-12 to 137 in 2026-01, and reached 156 in 2026-07 and 149 in 2026-08.
Paramount GR Holdings, LLC has a lift of 2.572 on 61 complaints.
ClarityPay, Inc. has a lift of 2.707 on 7 complaints, and SOLAR SERVICING HOLDINGS LLC has a lift of 2.492 on 20 complaints.
Affirm Holdings, Inc has a lift of 1.678 on 88 complaints, and Klarna AB has a lift of 1.651 on 24 complaints.
Templated share of recent narratives is 0.0 across 95 narratives, so the signals appear independently written.
30.3% of the 33-narrative AI sample involved financed goods or services not delivered as represented, and 27.3% involved lender or BNPL dispute handling failures.
21.2% of the sample involved undisclosed terms or questionable origination, and the mean AI severity was 3.58 out of 5.

checks.name: size
checks.reason: The brief frames the rise as spread across BNPL and point-of-sale lenders, and the lifts are all above 1 (Affirm 1.678 on 88, Paramount 2.572 on 61, Klarna 1.651 on 24, ClarityPay 2.707 on 7), so it does not blame one company whose lift fails to support it.

checks.name: templating
checks.reason: The templated share of recent narratives is 0.0 across 95 narratives, well below the 30% threshold.

checks.name: concentration
checks.reason: The top state TX holds only 15.0% of complaints, and the top company Affirm has 88 complaints with many other companies listed, so the signal is not confined to one state or one company.

checks.name: thin_evidence
checks.reason: The AI sample is 33 (above 15) and there are 95 recent narratives (above 10), and the named root causes (not delivered as represented 30.3%, dispute handling 27.3%, undisclosed terms 21.2%) together cover about 79% of the sample.

checks.name: seasonality
checks.reason: Monthly counts held at 122-156 since 2026-01 and the recent months 144, 156, 149 are not driven by a single peak month, and the latest month 149 is only slightly below the 156 peak after a single dip, so the rise is sustained.

skeptic.note: The rise is broad across companies, independently written, spread across states, backed by a relevant sample of 33, and sustained over recent months, so it passes all five checks.
